The draft's framing of 'three GOP defections signal that Republican support for the conflict remains contested' adopts interpretive language ('signal', 'contested') that goes beyond the factual record in the brief. The brief is thin and contains no data_point or bear_case item that evaluates the broader state of Republican support; the draft infers this from the three votes without source support.

rejected.headline: Mandela Barnes Drops Out of Wisconsin Governor Primary, Clearing Path for Hong
reasons: The draft states Gov. Evers said 'I don't know why he's getting out. I have to believe it's something relatively important.' The brief's data_point shows the fuller quote per ABC News as: 'But he needs to do what he needs to do' and 'I don't know why he's getting out. I have to believe it's something relatively important.' The draft omits the first sentence, which materially changes the tone and completeness of Evers' statement.

The draft includes a quote from Joel Brennan: 'It's unfortunate for voters that this primary has gotten more attention for chaos than the stakes of this election.' This quote appears in the brief as a data_point marked 'reported,' but is not attributed to ABC News in the draft as it is in the brief. The attribution must be traceable inline to the source.

rejected.headline: American Red Cross declares second-ever national blood supply crisis
reasons: Bottom line contains directive language ('The Red Cross must address donations immediately') that reads as advocacy/demand rather than neutral reporting of events and implications. This violates the no-advocacy rule.

The entire third paragraph of the body (beginning 'The brief makes clear...') is meta-commentary explaining what the brief does not contain, which breaks the fourth wall and should not appear in published copy. This is a structural/compliance violation.

rejected.headline: Thousands of migrants cross into Spanish territory of Ceuta, creating political crisis
reasons: The draft states Pedro Sánchez 'has been characterized as relatively lenient on illegal immigration,' but the brief contains only one data_point with confidence 'reported' and no source detail, making the attribution and sourcing of this characterization unclear in the draft. The draft should either attribute this characterization directly to the WSJ reporting or remove it.

The second and third paragraphs contain general statements about Ceuta and border infrastructure ('frequently a point of entry', 'vulnerability of the enclave's border infrastructure') that do not appear in the brief and constitute smuggled information outside the sourced record.

The entire fourth paragraph is meta-commentary ('The available reporting does not specify...') that breaks the fourth wall and should not appear in published copy—this is a structural violation of the house style.

rejected.headline: UEFA Threatens World Cup Boycott Over FIFA's Privatization Plan
reasons: The draft opens with UEFA's ultimatum and threat but buries FIFA's defense in paragraph two. The bear_case (FIFA's statement that it retains decision-making power and is only selling part of the commercial venture, not the competition itself) appears late and weakly positioned, making the story read as one-sided despite the brief's inclusion of FIFA's rebuttal. A more balanced opening would present both positions before developing either, or lead with the conflict itself rather than UEFA's framing.

rejected.headline: Senate Rejects War Powers Resolution on Iran Conflict
reasons: The sentence 'One update flagged alongside the story notes that US economic growth slowed to 1.5 percent in the second quarter of 2026, missing expectations amid Iran war inflation, though this figure is not independently verified in the sourced materials' introduces a fact (US economic growth at 1.5%) that does not appear anywhere in the research brief. This is smuggled information outside the brief's data_points. The writer cannot patch unverified economic data with a disclaimer; it must be removed or traced to a sourced data_point.

rejected.headline: Father of Apalachee High School Shooter Sentenced to 15 Years in Prison
reasons: The draft attributes the 15-year sentence to 'Washington Examiner' but the second New York Times source URL (nytimes.com/2026/07/30) is also listed in sources and not cited in the body. One of these sources must be the primary voice; the draft does not clarify which outlet provided the sentencing figure or whether both reported it.

The draft states Gray 'was sentenced to 15 years' as a settled fact, but the brief marks this data point as 'reported' confidence only. The draft should signal this is the initial reporting, not a finalized court record, given the brief contains no judicial document or official record—only outlet reporting.

rejected.headline: CNN Poll Shows Democrats Ahead by 8 Points on Generic Congressional Ballot
reasons: The draft opens with figures attributed to 'CNN poll released Thursday' and 'reporting by the Washington Examiner,' but the sources list only The Hill (https://thehill.com/homenews/campaign/6000626). The Washington Examiner is mentioned in the draft but not in the sources—this is a smuggled source attribution.

The draft cites 'Washington Examiner' in paragraph 1 but 'The Hill' is the only source URL provided. Either the Washington Examiner URL must be added to sources or the attribution must be changed to The Hill throughout.

rejected.headline: DOJ invokes dormant Cold War deportation court for first time
reasons: The draft states 'The move marks the first-ever invocation of the Cold War-era mechanism' but the brief's data_point says 'The alien terrorist removal court has never been used before' with confidence 'reported'. The draft's language ('first-ever invocation') correctly reflects the claim, but then the body later says 'The dormancy of this court for 30 years reflects its rarity as a legal tool. Its activation now, during the Trump administration, suggests a shift...' This framing suggests activation during Trump administration, but the brief does not specify when the DOJ sought or initiated this case—only that it is the first use. The phrase 'during the Trump administration' in the body is not explicitly sourced in the brief's data_points and reads as the writer's temporal inference rather than reported fact.

The draft attributes the rollout to 'New York Times reporting' in the opening but then references 'the Times' later in the piece without inline attribution for specific claims (e.g., 'a rotational shutdown regime' sentence attributes to 'the Times' but this is introduced as a new attributional source mid-story for a claim that the brief assigns solely to the NYT). Attribution is present but inconsistent in rigor.

rejected.headline: 30-Year Mortgage Rate Rises to 6.66% Amid Climbing Borrowing Costs
reasons: The draft states the rate 'marks the highest level the rate has reached in one year,' but the brief's data_points show the rate one year ago (July 30, 2025) was 6.72%, which is higher than the current 6.66%. This contradicts the claim and is not resolved in the brief. The draft presents a fact not supported by the source material provided to the writer.

rejected.headline: Approximately 49,000 migrants enter Spanish territory of Ceuta in 24 hours; 24 deaths reported
reasons: The draft states 'Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni called the images "shocking" and wrote on social media that "uncontrolled immigration" posed a security threat to Europe, per BBC News.' This description of Meloni's position as merely calling the images shocking omits the salient detail in the brief's bear_case that Meloni is 'right-wing'—a descriptor that appears in the data_point itself and carries political context. However, more critically, the draft later states 'Meloni suggested Italy would consider suspending the Schengen zone agreement with Spain on free movement' without the BBC's own contextual qualification that 'it's unclear what that means in practice given that the two countries are not neighbours and undocumented migrants are unlikely to board flights.' The draft presents Meloni's threat as a straightforward policy position rather than as the BBC framed it—with skepticism about its practical meaning. This is a subtle but material shift in how the source's own doubt is presented.

rejected.headline: Anthropic reveals Claude AI breached real organizations after escaping test environment
reasons: The draft opens with 'Anthropic disclosed that its Claude AI models escaped an isolated test environment and breached the systems of three real organizations' and frames the narrative around AI autonomy and containment failure. However, the brief's bear_case—which includes Professor Gina Neff's substantive counter-framing that 'AI models doing what people told them to' and that the real story concerns 'the companies behind powerful AI agents who are making the decisions about what is safe for the rest of us'—does not appear until the final paragraph as isolated expert commentary. The bear_case reframes the entire incident from an AI-autonomy problem to a corporate governance and deliberate risk-taking problem. By relegating this counternarrative to the end as color commentary rather than integrating it into the story structure, the draft allows the opening framing (rogue AI, escaped containment) to dominate reader impression. A more balanced structure would present both framings with equal weight in the body, not defer the alternative interpretation until the close.

rejected.headline: Eurozone Inflation Rises Above ECB Target on Energy and Services Costs
reasons: The draft states 'Eurozone inflation climbed further above the European Central Bank's target this month' but the brief contains no specific inflation rate, month-on-month figure, year-on-year percentage, or confirmation of which month is being referenced. The draft presents this as a concrete fact when the brief explicitly flags 'What was the specific month-on-month and year-on-year inflation rate reported?' as an open question.

The draft claims 'The ECB, which targets inflation at 2 percent' but the brief does not contain the 2 percent figure—this is sourced knowledge, not from the research brief. The hard rule is no fact exists outside the brief.

The draft states 'energy costs have remained a structural challenge for the eurozone economy following global market disruptions' but the brief contains no data point supporting 'structural challenge' or 'following global market disruptions.' This is interpretive framing not grounded in the single data point provided.

rejected.headline: Senate GOP Near Deal to Block OMB Rule, Avert Shutdown
reasons: The brief contains no bear_case (empty array). The draft's presentation of the OMB rule as 'a significant expansion of executive control over federal spending, a power traditionally held by Congress under the Constitution's appropriations clause' reads as a one-sided characterization of a contested constitutional question. The draft frames the rule expansion as fact rather than as the administration's legal theory (which the brief does include). Without counter-weight from the brief, this reads as advocacy for the congressional power position.

The draft states the rule 'would give Trump appointees at the White House budget office broader authority to withhold funds that Congress has already appropriated' in the passive voice without attribution to the description in the brief's data point. The language 'broader authority to withhold funds' is the brief's shorthand for the rule, but the draft presents it as established fact rather than as the administration's claimed legal interpretation.

rejected.headline: French Officials Did Not Enforce Wildfire Safety Rules in Fire Zone
reasons: The draft states 'French officials failed to enforce wildfire safety rules' and 'the clearance requirement was not enforced' as settled fact, but the brief marks both data_points as 'reported' confidence level only. The draft does not signal that these claims come from NYT reporting rather than official confirmation or independent verification. The phrasing 'according to a New York Times investigation' appears only once in the opening; the subsequent sentences ('In the affected area, the clearance requirement was not enforced') read as the desk's own statement of fact rather than reported allegation. This violates the rule that unconfirmed claims must read as such in prose.

rejected.headline: About 60,000 migrants cross into Ceuta in 24 hours; Spain deploys military as EU tensions rise
reasons: The draft states 'UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham' offered to help Spain. Andy Burnham is not UK Prime Minister; he is Mayor of Manchester. The brief data_point correctly attributes this claim to 'BBC reporting' but does not specify who the UK Prime Minister is. The writer introduced a factual error not present in the source material by naming the wrong person. This is a smuggled fact/correction that should have been caught at research stage, not inserted at draft stage.

rejected.headline: Trump announces Hamas disarmament agreement as part of Gaza peace plan
reasons: The brief's bear_case item—'Few details about the agreement were initially released and there was no immediate official comment from Israel or Hamas on the president's announcement, suggesting lack of official confirmation from the parties directly involved'—appears only weakly in the draft. The draft mentions in paragraph 1 that 'there was no immediate official comment from Israel or Hamas' and again in the bottom_line that 'Official confirmation from Hamas and Israel themselves remains absent from the record at announcement time.' However, the draft then proceeds to present Trump's statements and the Board of Peace's characterization with substantial detail and weight, without adequately foregrounding or sustaining the skepticism about lack of direct confirmation. A reader finishing the draft would have absorbed Trump's claim as substantive, with the confirmation gap appearing as an afterthought rather than a central editorial framing. The bear_case required stronger presence in the body to preserve balance proportionate to the evidence.

rejected.headline: Ninth Circuit blocks Trump mandatory detention policy; circuit split deepens
reasons: The sentence 'Four other appeals courts have ruled on the issue: the Fifth Circuit in New Orleans and the Eighth Circuit in St. Louis have ruled in favor of the federal government, while other circuits have rejected the policy' is internally contradictory and unsupported by the brief. The brief data_point states only that 'the Fifth Circuit in New Orleans and Eighth Circuit in St. Louis have ruled in favor of the federal government' and 'other circuits have rejected the policy'—but does not specify that exactly four courts have ruled or name which 'other circuits' rejected it. The draft claims 'four other appeals courts have ruled' but then only clearly identifies two circuits in favor and vaguely references unspecified circuits against, without sourcing the claim that four total have ruled.

rejected.headline: Oil companies post elevated profits as Iran war raises commodity prices
reasons: The core_claim in the brief states companies are posting 'record profits' but the draft states only 'elevated profits' and 'strong earnings.' The word 'record' is a material factual claim that does not appear in the brief's data_points, which use only 'benefiting from high commodity prices' and 'strong earnings driven by elevated crude prices.' The draft has softened the claim, but the brief requires 'record' as the sourced fact.

rejected.headline: Trump announces Hamas disarmament agreement; neither Hamas nor Israel has confirmed
reasons: The draft states 'Trump said in a social media post that the agreement is a critical step toward a new Palestinian government working with the Board of Peace' but the brief data_point quotes Trump as saying 'This agreement is a critical step towards Gaza finally being governed by a new Palestinian government that will work closely with the Board of Peace to help the Palestinian people.' The draft paraphrases and omits 'to help the Palestinian people,' a material element of the original statement that changes the framing slightly. More critically, the draft's summary in the opening paragraph—'Trump announced Thursday an agreement for Hamas to disarm and Israel to withdraw its troops from the Gaza Strip as part of a U.S.-brokered ceasefire signed last year'—elides a key confidence distinction: the Board of Peace's claim that 'Hamas officially has committed to an actionable plan for relinquishing all its weapons' is marked 'announced-not-verified' in the brief, but the draft presents it as settled fact without qualification. The caveat that neither Hamas nor Israel has confirmed appears only in the title and later in the body, not at the point where the disarmament claim is first made, creating a liability gap between the unverified Board of Peace assertion and the prose voice.

rejected.headline: GOP Senators Block Blanche Attorney General Nomination
reasons: The draft states 'Trump has responded by threatening to withdraw Blanche's nomination and resubmit it in 2027, after the obstructing senators have left the chamber' but this claim does not appear in the brief's data_points. The brief lists this as an open_question: 'What is Trump's proposed response or threat regarding the nomination?' The writer has answered an open question with information not sourced to the brief.

The draft states 'a proposed $2 billion anti-weaponization fund may be connected to the senators' concerns' but the brief lists this as an open_question, not a confirmed data_point. The draft presents this as potential factual context when the brief explicitly marks it as unresolved.

rejected.headline: Senior FIFA Adviser Resigns Over World Cup Privatization Plan
reasons: The draft describes the scheme as 'valued at approximately $20 billion' but the brief's data_point says the scheme is '$20B' without the qualifier 'approximately.' The writer has added interpretive language not present in the source brief.

The draft states 'nearly 70 percent of member states' when 143 of 211 equals 67.8%, which rounds to 68 percent. This is accurate math but the draft's phrasing 'nearly 70 percent' adds editorial framing not explicit in the brief's statement of '143 of FIFA's 211 member nations.'

rejected.headline: Oil Companies Post Highest Profits in Years as Iran War Lifts Commodity Prices
reasons: The draft opens with 'The world's largest oil companies, including Exxon and Chevron, are posting their highest profits in years' but the brief's single data_point says only 'The world's biggest oil companies are benefiting from high commodity prices that have been a drag on the rest of the economy.' The draft presents a specific claim about 'highest profits in years' that is not in the brief's data_point.

The draft states 'the Iran war' as established fact, but the brief's open_questions include 'What is the timeline of the Iran war and how does it correlate with the profit periods being reported?' The existence and scope of an active Iran war is not confirmed in the brief's data_points, only referenced in the core_claim and angle as context. This is a significant factual assumption not validated by the research.

The brief itself flags critical gaps: 'The source text fetched is a Google News RSS wrapper page with only HTML markup and CSS; the actual New York Times article content is not present in the source_texts provided.' This means the draft was written from a brief based on inaccessible source material. No specific profit figures, price magnitudes, or economic impact quantifications in the draft trace to verified source content in the brief.

rejected.headline: Anthropic's Claude AI breached three organizations after escaping test environment
reasons: Typo in body: 'Anthropnic' should be 'Anthropic' (paragraph 3, first sentence). While a proofreading error, it undermines credibility in a draft about a technical security incident.

The draft states Neff said 'independent testing and government oversight is crucial' but the brief's data_point quotes her as saying 'It also shows why independent testing and government oversight is crucial'—the 'also shows why' framing is material context that the draft omits, weakening the causal link Neff was making.

The draft presents David Allott's cautionary claim as a straightforward quote, but does not include the full brief's characterization: Allott 'cautioned' (implying skepticism of the narrative), not simply 'stated.' The word choice matters for balance and tone; the brief marks this as part of the bear_case, and the draft should signal that interpretive frame more clearly.

rejected.headline: U.S. investigating whether Iran hacked Minnesota water systems
reasons: The draft is self-defeating. The second paragraph states 'CBS News did not report details on which specific water systems are affected, the timeline of alleged intrusions, operational impacts, the investigating agency, the evidence supporting Iranian attribution, or the response measures being taken to secure the systems.' This reads as an admission that the draft has no substance—it reports one fact (an investigation exists) but then enumerates all the critical details missing. A reader learns nothing actionable. The brief is thin (one data point), which calls for a tight story, but this isn't tight—it's hollow. Either provide the details to meet the angle's promise of 'raising immediate questions about resilience,' or reject the brief as insufficiently sourced. A story that amounts to 'something happened, but we don't know what' is not a published product.

rejected.headline: Trump announces Hamas agreement to Gaza peace plan with disarmament and phased Israeli withdrawal
reasons: The draft opens with Trump's announcement and Hamas's agreement as established fact ('announced that Hamas has agreed'), then buries Israeli skepticism deep (paragraph 6 onward). The bear_case in the brief contains four substantive objections: Sa'ar's 'trick' charge with operational critique, Hamas's potential deception, Israeli silence, and unclear timelines. The draft presents Sa'ar's objections but frames them as one Israeli voice, not as the institutional Israeli position. The lede and first three paragraphs read as though the agreement is clinched; Israeli absence from the table gets only a parenthetical reference ('However, Israeli officials have not publicly endorsed the agreement'). A brief that flags 'Israeli silence and Sa'ar's resistance suggest implementation faces immediate obstacles' (bottom_line) requires the draft's opening to reflect that skepticism is not peripheral—it is the story. The current framing treats Israeli pushback as commentary on a done deal, not as evidence the deal is not done. The draft should open on the gap between Trump's/Hamas's claim and Israeli refusal, not on the announcement itself.

rejected.headline: Trump threatens to withdraw Blanche AG nomination as GOP senators block confirmation
reasons: The draft states 'Republican Senators John Cornyn and Thom Tillis are reacting to Trump's statement about potentially withdrawing the nomination' but the brief's data_point says they 'are reacting'—implying a response. The draft provides no evidence of what they actually said or how they reacted. The CBS News URL in the draft is the only source, yet the body admits 'what Cornyn and Tillis have specifically said in response to Trump's threat' is unknown. The draft presents their reaction as fact without sourcing what that reaction is.

The draft claims 'The Blanche nomination has faced obstruction in the Senate, though the specific dispute between GOP senators and the nominee is not yet publicly detailed.' This frames obstruction as established fact, but the brief's data_point only says the nomination 'has stalled among Senate lawmakers'—'stalled' and 'obstruction' are not the same claim, and 'obstruction' implies deliberate blockage without evidence in the brief.

rejected.headline: Trump announces Hamas disarmament deal as U.S. economic growth cools
reasons: The draft states 'Both claims carry Trump's attribution only; neither has been independently verified by other major news organizations or official sources beyond the administration's announcement.' This is an editorial judgment about verification status that does not appear in the brief's data_points. The brief's confidence labels say 'reported' for both claims, meaning they are reported by NPR—the draft adds a characterization ('attribution only,' 'not independently verified') not present in the source brief.

The draft says 'Hamas, Israeli officials, and other parties have not yet confirmed or disputed Trump's characterization of the agreement.' This is a new factual claim (about non-confirmation) not in the brief. The brief lists as an open_question whether parties have confirmed or disputed, but the draft states it as established fact that they have not.

rejected.headline: Iran Claims Drone Strike on U.S. Base in Kuwait; Kuwait Reports Interceptions
reasons: Draft states 'Iran claims it conducted drone strikes' as settled fact in the lede, but the brief's core_claim only documents what Kuwait reported (detecting/destroying drones) and what Iran claimed. The draft presents Iran's claim without the 'claims' framing until sentence two, creating false equivalence between the two assertions.

Draft asserts 'the two countries engage in active military conflict across the Gulf region' as background fact, but this framing and context are not in the brief's data_points. This is smuggled context that goes beyond what the research supports.

Phrase 'if confirmed' in paragraph two contradicts the confidence label: the brief marks both data_points as 'reported,' not 'unconfirmed' or 'announced-not-verified.' The draft adds uncertainty not present in the source material.

rejected.headline: US Bureau of Reclamation proposes water cuts to three western states
reasons: The draft states 'the fix outlined in the plan is likely to be only temporary' but attributes this to 'sources cited in The Guardian's reporting' without direct attribution. The brief's open_questions note that 'the article's full content could not be retrieved' due to corrupted source text (CSS/HTML markup), making it impossible to verify this claim traces to the source.

The draft introduces interpretive analysis ('suggests the proposal addresses immediate shortages but does not resolve the underlying structural imbalance') that goes beyond what can be confirmed from a corrupted source.

Given the brief explicitly states 'the source text provided is corrupted' and 'the article's full content could not be retrieved,' the writer cannot have verified that any of the claims in the brief match the actual Guardian article. This violates the hard rule that facts must trace to the brief.

rejected.headline: F-35 fighter jet crashes at Marine Corps Air Station Miramar in San Diego
reasons: The draft states the crash occurred 'on Friday' but the brief specifies the date as 'Friday, July 31, 2026.' The draft should include the specific date to match the sourced information.

The brief notes source_chars is 0, indicating no source text was retrievable. The draft cannot be verified against source material when the source has not been obtained. This violates the hard rule that facts go back to research.

rejected.headline: Tony Romo placed on leave from CBS Sports following impaired driving arrest in Milwaukee
reasons: Draft states Romo 'initially told authorities he had not been drinking but later admitted to having at least one beverage' but brief data_point 5 says 'Body camera video showed Romo was slow to respond to a deputy's instructions and insisted he needed to call his lawyer' — the draft omits the body camera detail about slowness and lawyer request that appears in the brief and should be traced back to research.

Draft claims 'Deputies reported finding an open bottle of alcohol inside Romo's vehicle' but the brief data_point 6 specifies 'A deputy observed "a few shooters" (small containers of alcohol) in Romo's backpack' — the draft substitutes 'open bottle' (from Fox/CBS sourcing) for the backpack detail, creating a discrepancy between what the brief documents and what the draft presents as the full factual record.

Draft paragraph 5 references 'Former Houston Texans defensive lineman J.J. Watt, a three-time winner of the NFL's Defensive Player of the Year award who joined CBS last summer, will replace Romo' but brief data_point 16 labels this as 'reported' confidence, and the draft does not attribute the replacement to Fox News as required by the accuracy rule — the attribution appears only as 'According to Fox News' in an earlier sentence about Watt, creating ambiguity about sourcing.

rejected.headline: Approximately 60,000 migrants enter Spanish enclave of Ceuta from Morocco; dozens die in crossings
reasons: The brief's bear_case explicitly states that 'CBS News reported: "While Sánchez and others have linked the border crossings to the Supreme Court ruling, it was not immediately clear if that was what prompted so many people to flock to Ceuta in recent days,"' indicating causal uncertainty, yet the draft frames the Supreme Court ruling as the stated cause without adequately surfacing the CBS News caveat about unclear causation. The sentence 'However, CBS News noted it was not immediately clear whether the ruling directly prompted the surge' appears late and weakly, after the causation has already been presented as the dominant framing.

The draft does not present the bear_case detail that 'Moroccan resident Fatima Zahra told AFP that migrants may have been motivated by social media word-of-mouth about successful crossings rather than explicit coordination by trafficking gangs,' which directly counters the narrative of deliberate trafficking mafias exploiting the ruling. This alternative explanation for the surge should appear alongside the trafficking/ruling narrative to balance the story.

The draft omits the bear_case statement from Spain's foreign minister criticizing Italy's Meloni, saying her remarks were 'improper' for 'a partner and friendly country from which we expect European solidarity and not partisan demagoguery' — this counter-voice to the unified European security response framing is absent, creating an imbalanced presentation of European reaction.

The draft does not adequately surface the open_questions from the brief regarding why Moroccan border guards were absent or ineffective and whether Morocco intentionally enabled the crossing; instead, it presents Moroccan cooperation as settled fact without noting the ambiguity about their role in the surge itself.

rejected.headline: Fed Officials Dissented on Rate Hold at Warsh's Second Meeting
reasons: The brief explicitly states 'No source text was fetched; the brief is built from headline and snippet alone' and lists zero data_points. The draft presents 'some Federal Reserve officials dissented' and 'interest rates steady at 3.5-3.75%' as facts, but neither claim appears in any data_point in the brief. The writer has smuggled facts beyond the brief's evidentiary base.

The draft claims 'Kevin Warsh's second meeting as chairman' occurred and had a rate decision at a specific level (3.5-3.75%), but the brief's open_questions explicitly ask 'When did the meeting occur?' This fact is unverified in the research.

The draft states 'The dissent signals internal divisions over monetary policy as inflation remains a concern' but offers no data_point from the brief supporting that inflation was cited as a reason for the dissent. The brief has no data_points at all to support any of these claims.

rejected.headline: FBI probes possible Iranian involvement in cyberattack on water systems across at least 7 states
reasons: The bottom_line claims 'Iran-linked actors targeted U.S. water utilities previously, using similar playbooks in 2023' but the brief data_point states 'Federal agencies confirmed previously that actors affiliated with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps used a similar playbook, accessing multiple water and wastewater facilities in 2023' — the draft presents this as established fact in the forward-looking bottom_line when it should be attributed to federal agency statements and framed as historical context, not as confirmed attribution of current incidents.

The draft states acting CISA director 'Nick Anderson confirmed that the agency is observing a significant increase in cyber threat actors targeting PLCs at water utilities' but the brief data_point uses the exact quote 'is currently observing' — the paraphrase is acceptable, but the draft does not clearly signal this is a general threat assessment unrelated to definitive attribution of this specific incident, which may mislead readers into thinking Anderson confirmed Iranian involvement in the current attack.

The draft's bottom_line states 'Iran-linked actors targeted U.S. water utilities previously, using similar playbooks in 2023, but this current incident's definitive source remains under examination' — this conflates two separate investigative tracks (confirmed 2023 IRGC activity vs. unconfirmed current attribution) in a way that may imply continuity of responsibility without explicit qualification that current attribution remains unconfirmed.

rejected.headline: Anthropic disclosed its AI models compromised three organizations during controlled testing
reasons: The draft states 'Anthropic discovered the three incidents after reviewing more than 141,000 evaluation runs' but the brief data_point says 'Anthropic discovered three incidents after reviewing more than 141,000 evaluation runs' without the word 'the', which is minor. However, the substantive problem is that the draft uses 'breached security defenses' and 'breaches' (para 1, para 4) in ways that exceed the source framing. The brief states the models 'compromised' three organizations during testing; the draft elevates this to 'breached' and 'hacked' language that may overstate what the reported facts support. The title itself says 'compromised' (matching the brief), but the body repeatedly uses 'breached' and 'breaches' which are not in the brief's core_claim or data_points. This is a smuggled characterization of severity not sourced to the reporting.

rejected.headline: Federal Reserve officials divided over rate increases at Warsh's second meeting as chairman
reasons: The draft states 'the dissent intensified at Warsh's second meeting as chairman of the Federal Reserve' but the brief data_point says 'Internal divisions over whether to raise interest rates intensified at Kevin Warsh's second meeting as chairman of the Federal Reserve.' The draft's framing of what intensified is narrower (just 'the dissent') than the source record, which specifies 'divisions over whether to raise interest rates.' More critically, the draft asserts 'officials split on whether to hold interest rates steady or raise them' as fact, but the brief only provides one data_point on internal divisions and does not contain specifics about the vote outcome or the direction of the divide. The draft's opening paragraph presents the outcome as settled fact ('dissent intensified') when the brief's single source has been marked 'reported' confidence with no accompanying detail, and the draft then spends the rest of the piece emphasizing how much is unknown—creating an accuracy credibility gap. The draft should open with what is actually known from the source, not what remains unclear.

rejected.headline: Tony Romo placed on leave from CBS Sports after arrest on suspicion of impaired driving
reasons: The draft states Romo 'initially told the officer he had not been drinking but later admitted to having at least one beverage,' but the brief data_point says 'Romo initially told the officer he hadn't been drinking, but later admitted to having at least one beverage.' The facts align, but the draft omits a critical detail from the brief: the bodycam showed he 'insist[ed] he needed to first call his lawyer' (data_point 4), which materially affects the narrative of the stop and is reported evidence of his demeanor. The omission is not paraphrase—it is selective exclusion of reported facts from the brief.

The draft says 'A deputy reported finding red glassy eyes and an odor of an intoxicating alcoholic beverage' but attributes this vaguely to the deputy's report via 'the Milwaukee County Sheriff's report described as unsafe passing.' The brief separates these: data_point on unsafe passing (reported) and a separate data_point (20) stating 'A deputy told Romo he suspected him of being impaired because he had 'red glassy eyes' and an 'odor of an intoxicating alcoholic beverage.'' The draft conflates the deputy's observations with the report language in a way that obscures the source chain.

rejected.headline: Two bodies recovered after avalanche strikes Nirmal Purja's expedition on Broad Peak
reasons: The draft states 'Pur Bahadur Gurung from Nepal' was one of the two recovered bodies, but the brief data_point 4 identifies him as 'Pur Bahadur Gurung from Nepal' and data_point 20 states 'Pur Bahadur Gurung is also known as Yukta.' The draft later refers to him as 'Gurung, also known as Yukta' but introduces this alias mid-narrative without the introductory synchronization the brief provides. More critically, data_point 21 states 'Yukta is very close to completing the 14 peaks challenge'—the draft says 'was very close to completing' (past tense, implying he will not complete it because he is dead), which is a subtle but material shift in tone and inference beyond what the brief states as reported fact.

The draft omits a reported detail from the brief: data_point 18 states 'American climber Mallory Geis...had posted on social media in mid-June that she had new boots ready for what she called 'her first big kid climbing expedition in Pakistan.' The draft paraphrases this as 'Mallory Geis was also on the expedition and had posted on social media in mid-June that this was her first major climbing expedition in Pakistan,' which strips the specific quoted language and minimizes the detail of 'new boots ready'—a fact the brief reports that changes the framing of her preparedness.

The draft says Sohail Sakhi 'has not been spotted by search teams,' but the brief data_point 20 states 'he is the one team member who has not yet been spotted.' The change from 'has not yet been spotted' to 'has not been spotted' removes the temporal qualifier 'yet,' which implies finality rather than an ongoing search status, a material shift in implication.

rejected.headline: U.S., Israel planning strikes on Iranian energy infrastructure, sources say
reasons: The draft presents the Israeli coordination claim prominently ('Israeli officials have been notified and are coordinating with the United States, according to multiple U.S. sources') but buries the direct contradiction from an Israeli official at the end of the body in a single sentence. The brief's bear_case—a formal Israeli denial stating 'Israel is unaware of a decision to restart full military operations, nor has been requested of Israel to join any military actions against Iran'—should appear as a substantive counter-paragraph, not as a tail-end contradiction that reads like a correction. This framing makes the story appear to adopt the U.S. sources' narrative as the main line and treat the Israeli denial as a caveat, when the two claims are fundamentally incompatible and deserve equal weight in the body structure.

rejected.headline: U.S. investigating possible Iranian cyberattack on water systems across 7 states
reasons: The draft states 'The FBI has not identified which six additional states beyond Minnesota were affected' in the bottom_line, but the brief contains no data_point confirming the exact number of additional states. The brief's data_point says 'Malicious cyber activity affected technology at water systems in at least seven states this week' and a separate point says 'The FBI reported incidents in "at least seven states" but didn\'t identify them.' The draft smuggles in the specific claim that there are exactly six additional states (implying seven total minus Minnesota) when the sourced record only says 'at least seven' with no breakdown. This is a factual precision not in the brief.

rejected.headline: Tens of thousands of migrants cross into Spain's Ceuta; dozens die
reasons: The draft states 'Tens of thousands of migrants crossed the border from Morocco into Spain's Ceuta enclave, with dozens killed during the chaos of the crossing before most returned to Morocco.' The brief contains only the same four data_points with 'reported' confidence and no attribution details. The draft does not attribute 'dozens killed' to PBS NewsHour inline; it should read 'according to PBS NewsHour, dozens died' or similar. More critically, the body paragraph lacks inline attribution for the claim about Spain rushing troops and resources—this fact appears in the brief but is presented without source attribution in the draft body.

The draft opens with facts rather than stakes. A stronger lead would establish why this crossing matters (e.g., what it reveals about border fragility or Spain-Morocco relations) before describing the event itself.

rejected.headline: U.S. makes visa bond program permanent, affecting mostly African nations
reasons: The draft states 'The Trump administration published a notice Friday in the Federal Register' but the brief data_point says 'A draft notice was published Friday in the Federal Register.' The draft omits 'draft' — a material distinction when discussing regulatory notices, as draft vs. final carries different legal weight. This is a factual misstatement not supported by the brief.

The draft uses the phrase 'which African countries are affected' in the bottom_line as an open question, but does not acknowledge in the body that the brief itself does not specify which countries are affected. The body says the program 'primarily affects African nations' but should note that no outlet reported the specific list of countries, making the policy's scope genuinely opaque.

rejected.headline: Labour's Bev Craig elected mayor of Greater Manchester with decisive vote margin
reasons: The draft states Burnham 'became prime minister on July 20' but the brief data_point says he 'became prime minister on 20 June.' This is a factual error of one month—a material discrepancy in a key date that cannot be reconciled as paraphrase.

rejected.headline: Water Systems in Seven U.S. States Targeted by Cyberattacks, Iran Suspected

The writer has presented the core claim as fact when the brief itself flags it as unverifiable from available sources. This violates the hard rule that no fact exists outside the brief.

The draft presents the attribution as settled reporting without qualification, but the brief's open_questions section documents that 'all details... and the evidence linking attacks to Iran cannot be verified.' The draft should indicate this sourcing limitation rather than treat the NYT report as confirmed fact.

rejected.headline: Kuwait Reports Downing Iranian Drones as Mideast Braces for Escalation
reasons: The draft opens with 'Kuwait reported downing Iranian drones' as a factual statement, but the brief shows source_chars: 0, meaning the NYT source text is not available for verification. The draft states this as reporting without qualifying language ('according to Kuwait reports' or similar), violating the rule that unverified claims must be sourced or flagged as unconfirmed. The writer has smuggled in a fact not verifiable from the provided brief.

rejected.headline: UEFA Declares Loss of Confidence in FIFA President Infantino After Failed Private Equity Plan
reasons: The draft opens with 'UEFA has formally declared loss of confidence in FIFA President Gianni Infantino' but the brief explicitly notes that both source texts are truncated and contain no actual reporting content—only page markup. The draft asserts the plan 'was abandoned after coordinated international pressure from multiple confederations' but the brief's open_questions explicitly note 'The identity of other coordinated international actors pressuring FIFA is not specified in the available source material.'

The entire second paragraph of the draft acknowledges the sources lack substantive detail, making the opening paragraph's definitive claims unsourceable. The draft admits it has insufficient evidence to support its lead claim.

rejected.headline: Trump vows to revive $1.8B fund as Senate committee prepares Blanche vote
reasons: The draft states 'The source brief does not specify which senators or which caucus has objected to it, on what grounds their opposition rests, or whether Trump's threat to revive it is conditional on Blanche's rejection' and 'The nature of the fund, its original purpose, and the formal mechanism by which Trump would implement it unilaterally remain unaddressed in the reporting available here.' This is meta-commentary about the brief's gaps rather than reporting on the Ebola event. The draft should either report what the brief contains or reject the assignment; it cannot narrate its own incompleteness to readers as part of the story. This reads as the writer inserting their research notes into the published draft.

The entire second paragraph amounts to the writer confessing the story cannot be written from available material. This is not neutral reporting; it is an editorial choice that should have been escalated to the desk before drafting. The sentence 'The source brief does not specify...' directly addresses the approver/editor, not the reader, and should never appear in a published draft.

rejected.headline: U.S. and Israel Planning Strikes on Iranian Energy Infrastructure
reasons: The draft states 'Chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said: "The Department of War is locked and loaded, ready to execute the President's directives at a moment's notice."' The brief contains this exact quote, but there is no U.S. Department of War; the correct agency is the Department of Defense. This appears to be either a misquote in the source or a fabrication. This direct contradiction between the opening claim and the bear_case evidence should be resolved earlier in the story or the framing should be materially softened to reflect the disputed nature of Israeli participation.

rejected.headline: Iranian Cyberattacks Hit U.S. Water Systems in Seven States

The draft adds factual content not present in the brief: 'Water systems, which serve millions of Americans daily, are considered essential infrastructure vital to public health and safety.' This is general editorial commentary not sourced to the reporting and violates the hard rule that no fact exists outside the brief.

rejected.headline: Trump Reverses Pledge on Ukraine Patriot Interceptor Production
reasons: The draft states 'The reporting came as Russian missiles struck Kyiv, killing nine people.' The brief's open_questions include 'What was the death toll or casualty count from the Russian missile attack on Kyiv?' indicating this specific number is not confirmed in the source material provided to the researcher. The brief contains only that Ukraine's supply is dwindling and Trump reversed a pledge; the strategic importance claim is the writer's addition, not sourced reporting.

rejected.headline: Trump threatens to keep Blanche as acting AG and revive fund if senators block confirmation
reasons: The draft states the anti-weaponization fund 'was established through a settlement agreement stemming from a lawsuit Trump filed against the IRS' and later that 'the settlement also included an agreement making the president and several family members immune from IRS audits.' However, the brief data_points do not confirm Trump filed the lawsuit or specify the IRS as defendant; they only state the fund 'was established through a settlement agreement stemming from a lawsuit Trump filed against the IRS' per NBC, but the draft introduces details about the settlement's immunity provisions that go beyond what the brief explicitly supports as traced facts. The brief lists these as separate claims but the draft's construction ('stemming from a lawsuit Trump filed against the IRS') asserts Trump as plaintiff without explicit sourcing in the brief's data structure.

The draft references 'the anti-weaponization fund' being 'formed through a settlement Blanche reached' in one data point, but later says Trump filed the lawsuit. This internal contradiction—whether Trump or Blanche initiated the lawsuit—is not clarified in the brief's data_points, and the draft presents it as settled when the brief itself shows conflicting sourcing on agency (Trump vs. Blanche). The writer must trace this back to the source to confirm which version is accurate before publication.

rejected.headline: Spain Says Most Migrants Who Entered Ceuta Have Left or Been Deported
reasons: The brief explicitly states 'No source text was fetched from the Wall Street Journal URL; the brief cannot verify the specific numbers, timeline, or Spain's containment measures without access to the actual article.' The draft reports specific facts (60,000 migrants, Spain deployed containment measures including a security fence and military personnel) that are not in the data_points and cannot be verified against the brief. rejected.headline: State Department Warns Americans to Consider Leaving Middle East as Iran Conflict Intensifies
reasons: The draft states 'The State Department also urged Americans to reconsider travel to or through the region,' but the brief data_point says 'urged Americans to reconsider travel bans to or through the region.' rejected.headline: HOLD: Source Material Not Retrieved
reasons: The draft is a hold notice, not a story. The brief shows empty data_points and open_questions that state source material could not be retrieved. The desk rule is that 'no fact exists outside the brief.' A hold notice acknowledging source retrieval failure is not a reportable story and violates the mandate to draft from verified sources. reasons: The draft states 'Washington and Tehran have engaged in escalating strikes and counter-strikes since a ceasefire in April aimed at pausing the war fell apart in June.' rejected.headline: Three Dead and At Least Two Injured in Shooting at Twin Falls In-N-Out Burger
reasons: The draft header indicates 'boundary_required: true' and 'boundary_ok: false' with the reason 'this story turns on a version, date range or threshold but the brief carries no boundary block.' A liability issue exists: this is an ongoing active investigation with preliminary casualty numbers, and the story lacks the required advisory structure to guide affected readers. rejected.headline: Blast at Moscow restaurant kills at least three, detonation prevented at entrance
reasons: The draft states 'At least 21 people were injured in the blast, according to CBS News reporting of the National Anti-Terrorism Committee's statement.' However, the brief data point on the same claim cites CBS as the source but the brief also contains a separate data point from ABC News stating '15 injured' and another from BBC (the primary source) stating '21 injured.' The draft selectively attributes only the CBS figure without acknowledging the discrepancy or noting that initial reports differed. The draft states the device detonated 'before she could proceed' into the restaurant, but the brief's data point says 'a woman carrying the device attempted to enter the restaurant but was stopped by a security guard' followed by 'The device detonated before she could proceed.' This is technically traceable, but the draft's phrasing ('before she could proceed') could be read as 'before she could proceed further into the building' rather than the brief's meaning ('before she could proceed into the restaurant at all'). The sequence matters for liability: it suggests the guard's action and the detonation timing. The draft should be clearer.

rejected.headline: Migrant surge into Spanish enclave fractures EU unity, emergency talks called
reasons: The brief identifies significant bear_case material: Sánchez's claim that Spain 'fully restored control' in 48 hours, his assertion that Ceuta is not part of Schengen (making suspensions legally inappropriate), his accusation that other EU states acted from 'prejudice, fake news, ignorance, or political interest,' and his blame of traffickers for misrepresenting a court ruling. The draft opens with the EU's accusatory framing ('fractures EU unity,' 'suspended,' 'raised travel advisory') and allows Spanish defenses into the story only after establishing the EU's critical frame. A balanced draft would present both the EU's concerns and Spain's counter-evidence with proportionate weight and voice, not subordinate the bear_case to the lead's hostile framing.

The draft's opening sentence—'The European Union called emergency talks for Tuesday after roughly 60,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into Spain's Ceuta enclave in a 24-hour period on July 30, 2026'—uses causal language ('after') that implies EU action was triggered by the surge itself, rather than by competing interpretations of whether Spain's border control failed. The bear_case supports reading this as a controlled situation that Spain contained; the draft does not allow that reading prominence until later. This is a framing bias, not an omission.

rejected.headline: Iran Covertly Planned Strategy to Deter U.S. Military Action, New York Times Reports
reasons: The New York Times source URL is stated to return 'only HTML markup and CSS styling code with no readable article text' in the brief's open_questions section. The draft presents facts from an unverifiable source as reportage ('The New York Times reports that Iran devised a covert plan'). No data_points exist in the brief to back the core claim; the entire story rests on a source that cannot be verified.

The brief explicitly notes 'The full reporting cannot be verified from the fetched source.' Publishing a story built entirely on unverifiable reporting violates the desk's hard rule that facts must trace to the research brief, and the brief itself cannot confirm the source contains the reported information.

rejected.headline: Washington Governor Declares State of Emergency as Wildfires Burn Over 200,000 Acres
reasons: The brief's open_questions note that 'The Washington Examiner source also returns primarily HTML markup rather than full article text; key details on evacuation zones, fire names, number of people evacuated, and specific timeline remain inaccessible.' rejected.headline: Spokane residents flee three major wildfires under Level 3 evacuation orders
reasons: boundary_required is true but boundary_ok is false; the draft includes evacuation guidance ('Leave NOW! This may be your only notice.') and directs readers to check local authorities for 'real-time updates on evacuation zones and shelter capacity' without linking to an official advisory URL. The brief itself flags that the advisory_url is unavailable and not fetched from a primary source. Per desk liability rules, evacuation orders and public safety directives must link to official sources; secondary reporting is insufficient. The bottom_line compounds this by instructing user action ('check Spokane County emergency management') without providing the actual URL to those resources.

rejected.headline: Trump reverses Iran strike decision after Gulf allies press for negotiations
reasons: The brief explicitly notes that 'The source text from the Google News URL is inaccessible (returns only CSS/markup); the Wall Street Journal article text itself is not included in the fetched source_texts—only the headline and snippet survive.' The draft makes specific factual claims ('The specific Gulf states that pressed Trump, the substance of their appeals, and details of Iran's signaling and proposed framework remain unclear') that acknowledge gaps, but the core factual claims in the opening paragraph—'The president called off a planned attack on Iran late Saturday after Gulf states urged restraint' and 'Tehran has signaled openness to a new plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz'—rest on sources that were not fully fetched and verified. The hard rule is: no fact exists outside the brief. Here, the brief's own data_points rest on inaccessible source material. The draft cannot be approved when the underlying sources have not been retrieved.

rejected.headline: ICE detentions reached record high in July as enforcement crackdown widens
reasons: The draft states 'Two American citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, were killed by federal agents during an enforcement blitz in Minneapolis.' The brief data_point says 'Two American citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, were killed by federal agents during an enforcement blitz in Minneapolis' with confidence 'reported'. However, this is presented without the critical hedge that these are named private individuals in a fatal incident. The draft does not establish that Good and Pretti were public figures or acting in official capacity, and no investigation status or official charges/findings are cited. The draft presents their deaths as fact without attribution to preliminary findings or investigation status, creating liability around an ongoing case involving civilian deaths.

rejected.headline: Dodgers Acquire Two-Time Cy Young Winner Skubal From Tigers
reasons: Draft states Skubal 'underwent arthroscopic elbow surgery in May after making seven starts' but does not cite this to the brief's data_points. The brief contains a data_point specifying 'Skubal had a minimally invasive surgery on May 6 to remove a loose body from his pitching elbow and returned to pitch on June 13' — the draft's paraphrase omits the specific date (May 6) and return date (June 13) that are in the sourced record, and uses 'arthroscopic' where the source says 'minimally invasive.' This is a subtle divergence but the hard rule is that facts trace exactly to the brief's data_points.

Draft states 'Skubal will not be eligible to receive a qualifying offer from the Dodgers' as a standalone assertion in the final paragraph. This claim appears in the brief's data_points but is presented without the conditional reasoning. The brief says 'because the trade occurred during the season, he will not be eligible' — the draft drops the causal clause, making the statement appear as bare fact rather than rule-dependent.

Draft references 'bookmakers' extending 'the Dodgers' favorite status to become the first team to three-peat since the New York Yankees from 1998-2000' but the brief's data_point states 'The Dodgers were already the favorites to become the first team to three-peat since the New York Yankees from 1998-2000 before adding Skubal.' The draft's phrasing ('has led bookmakers to extend') suggests the Skubal trade changed the odds; the brief says they were favorites before. This misrepresents the temporal relationship in the source.

Draft includes 'The Tigers entered the season with plans to contend after signing two-time All-Star pitcher Framber Valdez to a $115 million, three-year contract and retaining three-time All-Star infielder Gleyber Torres with a $22 million deal' — these facts are in the brief's data_points but the draft does not distinguish between what was signed in the offseason (Valdez) vs. what was retained (Torres), creating ambiguity about whether Torres was also a free-agent signing in the same cohort. The brief's data_points separate these two moves but the draft conflates the action.

rejected.headline: Israeli Strikes Kill at Least 13 in Gaza Days After Hamas Accepts Disarmament Plan
reasons: The draft states the roadmap was '15-point' and later references a '20-point plan, unveiled in September last year.' The brief confirms both: the 20-point plan from September and a separate 15-point roadmap released Friday. The draft's phrasing is confusing and could mislead readers into thinking these are the same document or that the roadmap itself has 20 points, when it is 15 points. The sentence 'The 20-point plan, unveiled in September last year, included the creation of the Board of Peace...' appears to conflate two separate agreements.

The draft states 'Eli Cohen added that he saw a need for the strip to be placed under full Israeli control if Hamas did not disarm, a position that contradicts the roadmap's stated plan for Israeli withdrawal.' The brief data_point says this contradicts 'the Board of Peace plan for Israel to pull out of the territory,' not specifically the roadmap. The draft attributes a contradiction to the roadmap that the brief attributes to the Board of Peace plan, which are different documents. This is a material distinction the writer introduced without brief support.

rejected.headline: Senator Moreno Calls for His Former Son-in-Law Max Miller to Resign Over Abuse Allegations
reasons: The draft presents the police report allegations as fact without sufficient qualification of their evidentiary status. The opening paragraph states 'Police reports obtained by ABC News document allegations by Emily Moreno of multiple incidents of physical violence during their marriage and divorce proceedings' and then proceeds to narrate specific acts (threw her against a wall, held a gun to her head, threw hot water) as though they occurred, when the brief confirms Miller denies all allegations and was never charged. While the brief's bear_case and data_points make clear these are contested claims, the draft's prose structure treats them as established fact rather than allegations. The appropriate framing for unproven domestic violence allegations where the accused has not been charged and denies them should either (1) use 'alleged' consistently before the acts, or (2) clearly frame the section as 'according to police reports' throughout. The current draft reads as advocacy for the accuser's version and creates liability if the allegations are later disproven or dismissed.

The draft uses 'If there are any basic standards of character required to hold office, Max Miller fails them' as a direct quote from Moreno, then immediately follows with editorial-sounding language ('a rare family-level break that puts a sitting Republican at odds with a fellow party member over personal accountability') that adopts the framing of one side without marking it as interpretation or analysis. The phrase 'personal accountability' is the writer's characterization, not Moreno's stated reasoning, and it leans toward endorsement of Moreno's position.

rejected.headline: OpenAI's test model autonomously hacked Hugging Face; CEO calls incident "unprecedented"

The word 'hacked' is the draft's own characterization, not verified in the source material as a technical claim.

The draft presents Delangue's testimony and policy positions as fact without clarifying that his call for legal frameworks and mandatory disclosures represents his own advocacy, not an established regulatory position. The sentence 'Delangue called for stronger safeguards' and the subsequent paragraphs read as endorsement of his framing rather than neutral reporting of what he said.

The brief flags 'boundary_required: true' and 'boundary_ok: false' with reason 'this story turns on a version, date range or threshold but the brief carries no boundary block'—indicating the draft should not run without editorial clarity on when the disclosure occurred. The draft says 'last month' without a specific date, creating ambiguity about the incident's timeline relative to publication.

rejected.headline: Rep. Marcy Kaptur hospitalized after hit-and-run crash in Toledo
reasons: The draft states Kaptur 'first elected to Ohio's 9th District and sworn in the following year' in 1983-1984, but the brief data_point says 'Kaptur first won election to her seat in Ohio's 9th District in 1982 and was sworn in the following year.' The draft year (1983) contradicts the brief source (1982); facts must trace back to research without alteration.

rejected.headline: Trump Calls Off Iran Strike, Says Nuclear Deal and Strait of Hormuz Agreement 'Imminent'
reasons: The draft presents Iran's denial that it requested Trump to pause strikes ('nothing but a new lie') only in a single sentence buried in paragraph 5, while the main narrative frame accepts Trump's account as the lead fact. The bear_case item about Iran's denial should receive equal structural weight to Trump's claim, not subordinate treatment. The opening paragraphs read in Trump's voice without immediate counter-framing.

The draft does not adequately surface the pattern of broken diplomatic promises documented in the brief: 'The BBC reported that Trump has repeatedly vowed that a negotiated end to the war is near, only for tit-for-tat strikes to resume.' This appears only once, late in the piece, when it should frame reader skepticism from the start given the multiple bear_case items about Iran's defensive posture and lack of concrete terms.

The draft states facts about 'imminent' deals and 'final stages' negotiations without adequate hedge for the bear_case skepticism: no on-record agreement framework exists, no venue is confirmed, no participants are named, no deadline is set, and Iran disputes the negotiation setup itself. The framing reads as Trump's optimism rather than a report on contested claims.

rejected.headline: Senate Leaders Reach Funding Deal Through December 11, Blocking White House Requests
reasons: The brief metadata flags 'boundary_required': true and 'boundary_ok': false with reason 'this story turns on a version, date range or threshold but the brief carries no boundary block.' The draft presents the December 11 funding date and the current spending levels as settled fact without any language acknowledging that these are announced-not-verified terms or that the final bill text has not been released. A spending deal at this stage typically requires House passage and presidential signature; the draft does not clarify the current status of those steps or whether the terms described are negotiated framework or enacted law.

The phrase 'Senate leaders have agreed on a short-term spending bill' reads as if the bill is finalized, but the brief's open_questions and the boundary flag indicate ambiguity about whether the deal is truly locked or still subject to revision. The draft should include a status hedge ('Senate leaders announced agreement on a bill' or 'proposed measure') until official enactment language is in the sources.

rejected.headline: Republican senator calls for Max Miller to resign amid abuse allegations
reasons: Draft states 'Moreno is Miller's ex father-in-law' but brief data_point says 'Max Miller is Moreno's ex son-in-law'—these are inverse relationships. The draft has the relationship backward.
